contents.name: Contents: `4. Turing degrees`, with §§4-2 `Computation with oracle`, 4-3 `Relativization of proofs`, 4-4 `Use property`, 4-5 `Turing degrees`, and 4-6 `Turing jump`
1. `Finite strings`, Definition 1.1 (finite binary strings), and Definition 1.2 (prefix notation for strings and infinite binary sequences)
2. `Computation with oracle` and Definition 2.1 (Turing functionals)
Definition 2.2 (X-computable and X-c.e. sets)
Example 2.3 (an oracle whose enumeration dominates diagonal halting times computes the halting set)
3. `Relativization of proofs` and Theorem 3.1 (the diagonal halting set relative to X is not X-computable)
4. `Use property`, Proposition 4.1 (Use property)
Definition 4.2 (the partial use function of a functional)
contents.reason: The selected page needs the finite-query witness but not a separate use-function calculus; its modulus and continuity applications belong to later priority and randomness developments.

contents.name: Remark after Definition 4.2 (a functional as a consistent c.e. set of finite-oracle triples)
Exercise 4.3 (effective composition of relative computations)
5. `Turing degrees` and Definition 5.1 (Turing reducibility and strict reducibility)
Definition 5.2 (Turing equivalence and Turing degrees)
Exercise 5.3 (degree order is independent of equivalent representatives)
Exercise 5.4 (Turing degrees are stable under finite variation)
contents.reason: Finite-variation invariance is useful later in priority constructions, but it is not a prerequisite for the selected quotient order, join, jump, or reduction-separation proofs.

contents.name: Proposition 5.5 (every Turing degree is countably infinite)
contents.reason: The cardinality of an individual degree does not enter the planned reducibility, join, or jump proofs and would open a separate set-theoretic counting discussion.

contents.name: Definition 5.6 (effective even/odd join)
Proposition 5.7 (the effective join induces the least upper bound of two degrees)
Exercise 5.8 (monotonicity of effective join under Turing reducibility)
6. `Turing jump` and Definition 6.1 (X-prime as relative diagonal halting)
Exercise 6.2 (jump monotonicity)
Proposition 6.3 (X is strictly below X-prime)
Exercise 6.4 (one uniform functional computes X from X-prime)
Definition 6.5 (Turing-complete and incomplete degrees)
contents.reason: Completeness classification is a different degree-theoretic topic; the page uses only relative c.e. completeness and finite jumps, already given precise local definitions.

contents.name: 5. `Computably dominated degrees`, Proposition 4.7 (every noncomputable Delta_2^0 set is hyperimmune)
Definition 5.1 (computably dominated sets and degrees)
5.1. `Truth-table reduction`
Definition 5.9 (truth-table reducibility by a functional total on every oracle)
Definition 5.10 (computable finite truth tables)
Theorem 5.11 (equivalent total-functional, truth-table, and computable-use-bound formulations)
Theorem 5.12 (computable domination iff every Turing reduction to the oracle is truth-table)

contents.name: Contents: Chapter 5 `Relativized computation and Turing degrees`, with §§5.1 `Turing reducibility`, 5.2 `The jump operator`, 5.3 `Limit computable sets`, and 5.4 `Incomparable degrees`
5.1 `Turing reducibility` and Definition 5.1.1 (partial and total A-recursive functions)
Definition 5.1.2 (indexed partial A-computable functions)
Definition 5.1.3 (Turing reducibility and T-equivalence)
Proposition 5.1.4 (Use Principle)
Definition 5.1.5 (use of a computation)
contents.reason: Only finiteness of the actual query transcript is needed here; an independent numerical use function would add machinery reserved for later finite-injury arguments.

contents.name: 5.2 `The jump operator` (definition of A-prime, A is many-one reducible to A-prime, and iterated jumps)
Proposition 5.2.1 (many-one and relative-c.e. characterizations of Sigma levels; Delta_(n+1)^0 equals sets Turing reducible to the n-th jump)
5.3 `Limit computable sets` and Definition 5.3.1
Proposition 5.3.2 (Shoenfield Limit Lemma)
5.4 `Incomparable degrees`
contents.reason: Constructing incomparable degrees requires the priority argument developed on the later page devoted to priority methods, rather than this foundational degree-and-jump page.
